area: Area VII. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can fly and explain a power-off 180° accuracy approach from the right seat, touching down on or within 200 feet beyond the point, and you can coach a learner's energy judgment at the key positions, spot their errors early and decide when the approach must become a go-around.
why: Estimating how far the airplane will glide is the real basis of every power-off accuracy approach, and it is the same judgment a pilot needs to choose a field in an actual emergency [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. The AIH singles out this maneuver: an instructor should anticipate the learner's landing errors, because learners may know not to trade a safe landing for accuracy and still not be ready to apply it [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

warmup: Think first: your commercial learner has flown five power-off 180s today. Three ended short of the point and two were rescued with a long, steep slip at 100 feet. The airspeed was on target at every key position. Before you blame the slip technique, what was decided on the downwind leg that made all five go wrong, and what one question would you ask at the next downwind key to find out?

The point on base where the spot appears about 45° from the nose; from there the approach is flown like a 90° power-off approach [[24:197|AFH 9-26]] [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].
The speed that gives the greatest forward distance for a given loss of altitude in still air, at the highest lift-to-drag ratio [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].
A stabilized, power-off descent at the best glide speed [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
The speed that keeps the airplane aloft longest; it is generally a few knots below best glide and covers less distance [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Planning, monitoring and controlling altitude and airspeed targets in relation to the airplane's energy state [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

The throttle: thrust above drag adds total energy, thrust below drag removes it [[24:90|AFH 4-4]]. The elevator only trades energy between altitude and airspeed, and drag devices can only add drag [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].
Angling the base leg away from or toward the runway to lose or save altitude when conditions are not as expected [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].
Bank one way, opposite rudder the other, so the airplane keeps its flight path while sinking faster without gaining airspeed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
Wing lowered and just enough opposite rudder to stop a turn, so the longitudinal axis stays parallel to the path; used to cancel crosswind drift [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
The point where full rudder is needed to hold heading; more bank would turn the airplane [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
The belief that the approach is sure to end in a safe landing; with pride, one of the two causes of a delayed go-around [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

chunks.title: The maneuver, its purpose and your standard

body.p: A power-off accuracy approach is a glide, with the engine idling, through a set pattern to touch down on a given point or within a set distance beyond it. Its objective is the judgment and procedures to fly the airplane to a safe landing without power [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. The 180° version starts from a point on the downwind leg, abreast of the spot, and adds a 90° turn without power to reach the base key at the right height. It needs more planning and judgment than the 90° approach [[24:197|AFH 9-26]] [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

Why it matters when you teach: the real basis of all power-off accuracy work is estimating gliding distance [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. A pilot who knows the normal glide angle can predict where the airplane will land along a ground path, and that skill drives the choice of a field in an actual emergency [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. So every 180° you teach is also a forced-landing lesson.

callout.text: ACS AI.VII.O.S8: “Touch down at a proper pitch attitude, within 200 feet beyond or on the specified point with no side drift and with the airplane’s longitudinal axis aligned with and over the runway centerline or landing path, as applicable.” Landing even a few feet short of the point is outside the standard.

ACS Appendix 3: a go-around because you cannot complete this Task within the tolerances is unsatisfactory. A go-around for runway safety concerns beyond the control of you or the evaluator is not. Neither of you may sacrifice safety and force a landing to complete the Task. The AFH says the same in plain words: never sacrifice a good approach or landing just to land on the spot [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

body.p: Single-engine turboprops are a passing case: some sink too fast at flight idle. In training, do not feather; set enough power to give the performance expected with the propeller feathered [[24:196|AFH 9-25]] (ACS Appendix 3).

check.q: The examiner names a point 800 feet past the threshold. Your mains touch 780 feet past it, on the centerline with no drift. Does that meet AI.VII.O.S8?
check.a: No. The window runs from the point to 200 feet beyond it, 800 to 1,000 feet here, and 780 feet is short of the point (ACS AI.VII.O.S8).

chunks.title: The glide: speed, angle and distance

body.p: Best glide speed gives the greatest forward distance for a given loss of altitude in still air, at the maximum lift-to-drag ratio. Glide faster or slower and drag rises, so the glide ratio gets worse [[24:83|AFH 3-22]]. A constant glide speed is normally held, because changing it ruins any attempt to judge gliding distance and the landing spot [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

Height versus angle: up to about 1,000 feet, height can be judged by eye with fair accuracy; above that, ground features merge and the altimeter is the best aid. But the AFH says knowing the normal glide angle matters more than knowing height in feet [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Teach the learner to judge the angle down to the spot, not to chase a number.

bullets: Above best glide: nose down means faster and steeper; nose up means slower and shallower [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Below best glide: nose down means faster and shallower; nose up means slower and much steeper [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. This is the half learners get wrong.
Raise the nose too far and the airplane settles rapidly from low speed and too little lift, which is why a glide is never stretched [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].
Weight does not change the glide angle at the proper speed; a heavier airplane glides faster and covers the same distance in less time [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Flaps, gear and cowl flaps add drag, so the nose must come down to hold speed and the glide gets steeper and shorter [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Minimum sink speed is a few knots slower and keeps the airplane up longer, but covers less distance [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

body.p: Teaching the normal glide: the learner should memorize the attitude against the horizon, the sound of the air and the feel of the controls. Point out that rising sound means rising speed, and have the learner use sound, sight and feel consciously until they become habit [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Expect slight left rudder in the glide and larger control movements, because slipstream and P-factor are gone while the built-in compensation remains [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

callout.text: Slow and sinking? Nose down to go farther. Below best glide, lowering the nose flattens the path [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

check.q: Your learner is 8 knots below best glide on base and the spot is creeping up the windshield. They ease back on the yoke. What happens, and what should they do instead?
check.a: Below best glide, pitching up greatly steepens the descent, so they will land even shorter [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Lower the nose to regain best glide, which flattens the path, then shorten the base or go around [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

chunks.title: Energy management and a stabilized approach at idle

body.p: Energy management means planning, monitoring and controlling altitude and airspeed against the airplane's energy state. Mismanaged energy contributes to loss of control in flight, CFIT and approach-and-landing accidents, the three most common fatal accident types [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. Total energy is altitude plus airspeed [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

Normally the throttle is the total energy controller and the elevator distributes energy between altitude and speed. When thrust is less than drag, total energy decreases, and high lift and drag devices can only increase drag [[24:90|AFH 4-4]]. Application: once the throttle closes at the downwind key, no control in the cockpit can add total energy back. Every choice after that is about how fast it drains (flaps, slips) and how far the path is (pattern shape), while the elevator trades height and speed. Only the air can change it from outside: a gust or windshear can raise or cut the airspeed [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

body.p: What stabilized means here: the AFH lists glide path, heading, airspeed, configuration, descent rate, power and briefings, and says to focus on the elements rather than their order or meeting every criterion [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. In this maneuver power is fixed at idle and pitch controls airspeed [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. The aim of the final approach is a descent angle that reaches the aiming point at a speed giving a predictable float, so both angle and speed must be held accurately [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

Make it repeatable: closing the throttle with the same airspeed and height each time makes the maneuver predictable [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. A learner who arrives at the key 10 knots fast one lap and 100 feet low the next is not practicing judgment, only recovery.

callout.text: Plan slightly high. An approach planned slightly high in the current configuration is sure to make the aiming point [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]. Extra energy can be bled off with drag; a shortfall cannot be made up without power.
The stabilized-approach gate still applies: in a typical piston airplane in the pattern, go around at once if the approach becomes unstabilized below 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

check.q: At the base key your learner is on glide speed but clearly higher than usual. Name the energy error and two fixes that work with the throttle closed.
check.a: Too much total energy. Add drag or path: lower flaps earlier, dog-leg away from the runway or S-turn on base, or slip briefly on final [[24:196|AFH 9-25]] [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

chunks.title: The key positions: where to close the throttle and how to judge

head: Point

Source
rows: Downwind
Heading parallel to the runway, at the normal pattern distance; start usually no higher than 1,000 feet AGL except in large airplanes
Downwind key
Abreast of the spot: throttle closed, altitude held while slowing to the recommended glide speed or 1.4 VSO
Glide entry
Prop forward if equipped, back pressure to hold altitude as speed decays, then set the glide attitude and trim

Uniform turn, medium or slightly steeper bank; bank and amount of turn depend on glide angle and wind

Spot about 45° from the nose; fly it like a 90° approach: flaps as needed, turn to the centerline, 1.3 VSO on final, trim

body.p: A key position is not the goal. It is only a convenient point in the air from which the pilot judges what to do so the landing happens at or just beyond the point, and it should suit the available altitude and wind. From the key on, the pilot keeps evaluating [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. Inexperienced pilots often tie the base key to a tree or crossroad at a certain height, then are lost without it. Vary altitude and location as much as practical [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

Build it in blocks: the glide from the base key through the 90° turn to final is the last part of every accuracy landing [[24:196|AFH 9-25]], and the 180° is an extension of the 90° [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]. Teach the 90° from base first, then add the downwind segment.

callout.text: Demonstration patter at the downwind key (application): 'Abeam the point. Throttle closed. Holding altitude while the speed comes back. Glide speed: nose down, trim. Now I judge: the point is at this angle; with this wind I will turn base now.' Short, then quiet while you fly.

check.q: Today's point is the 1,000-foot markers, but your learner closes the throttle when the runway numbers pass the wingtip. What has happened to the plan?
check.a: On downwind the numbers come after the markers, so the throttle closed past the downwind key, which is abreast of the point [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]. The glide now has farther to go, so expect a low approach; turn base promptly and shorten the base.

chunks.title: Wind and air: reading them leg by leg

body.p: Wind changes gliding distance over the ground: a tailwind makes the airplane glide farther because of the higher groundspeed, and a headwind makes it glide less far [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Density altitude matters too: the airplane lands at the same indicated airspeed as at sea level but a higher true airspeed, and at 5,000 feet the minimum landing distance is about 16 percent greater [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

body.p: Tailwind (R2c): it sits on every downwind of this maneuver and it hides on base. An unrecognized tailwind component on base raises groundspeed and leads to a late turn, an overshoot and the temptation to skid [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. If the landing itself is downwind, a 10-knot tailwind adds about 21 percent to landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

Teaching it: all pilots should learn to find wind direction and estimate its speed from the windsock, smoke, dust or water [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. Ask the learner on every downwind where the wind is and what it will do to the base leg, before the key arrives (application).

check.q: A hot afternoon at a 5,000-foot field. Your learner flies the same indicated speeds as at home. What changes about the touchdown?
check.a: Same indicated airspeed, but a higher true airspeed and groundspeed, so the landing distance is about 16 percent greater than at sea level [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

chunks.title: Shaping the glide: flaps, slips, S-turns and dog-legs

body.p: Square patterns show good planning but are not required. When conditions are not as expected, the pilot may dog-leg away from or toward the runway on base, use S-turns, slips, early or late flaps, fly below best glide, or slightly above it in a headwind, to reach the aiming point and touch down where planned [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. The AFH tells instructors to stress slips, flaps, base-leg position and the turn to final as the ways to correct misjudged altitude and glide angle [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

bullets: Configure correctly (S6): before-landing checklist on downwind, including the gear in a retractable [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]; prop to full increase rpm at the key [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].
Flaps set both the landing spot and the descent angle [[24:172|AFH 9-1]]. Up to about 15° they add mostly lift and the airplane tends to balloon; beyond 15° drag rises sharply [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
Extend in increments and be ready to re-trim after each change [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
Premature flap or gear extension is a listed error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]. Delay full flaps until adding them clearly will not put you short of the point [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].
Never retract the flaps to reach the spot [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]; it can cause a sudden loss of lift and an excessive sink rate [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

body.p: The forward slip loses altitude without gaining airspeed. Bank sets the amount of slip and so the sink rate; power is normally at idle and the elevator controls airspeed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Full rudder is the practical slip limit [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. To recover, level the wings and release the rudder together while setting the glide attitude; a sudden rudder release swings the nose and builds speed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Unlike retracting flaps, a slip can be taken out without penalty [[24:185|AFH 9-14]].

head: Forward slip operations (R7)
What the sources say
What you teach
rows: Fuel flowage
Some airplanes limit slips by time or fuel quantity, because uncoordinated flight can force fuel to one side of a tank and starve the engine [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
Brief the POH limit before the lesson; keep slips brief, as the AFH technique describes [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]
Tail stalls with flaps

For a clean airplane, the AFH slip section says only that there may be recommendations or limitations on slips with flaps extended, for aerodynamic reasons, and to consult the AFM/POH [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Flaps may change the wing's downwash on the horizontal tail and alter the tail-down force, so pitch behavior with flaps depends on the design; beyond 15° some high-wing airplanes get a significant nose-up pitching moment [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. The tail normally pushes down [[1:113|PHAK 5-16]]. No AFH or PHAK page describes a tail stall in a clean airplane slipping with flaps.

Follow the POH note on slips with flaps; if it limits them, slip only at the flap settings it allows, or fix the height earlier with path and flap timing [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. If the POH is silent, say so to the examiner and do not invent a rule. The AI.VII.M (slip to a landing) lesson covers this risk in more depth.
Airspeed control
The elevator controls airspeed in the slip, and the airspeed indicator may have considerable error because of pitot and static port location [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
Judge the slip by attitude, airflow sound and control feel [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]; reacting to false airspeed readings is a listed error [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]

callout.text: Icing only: tailplane stall symptoms and recovery appear only in icing material. With ice on the tail, the tail may stall after the flaps are lowered [[23:92|IFH 4-15]], and the IFH recovery is to retract the flaps to the previous setting with nose-up elevator [[23:93|IFH 4-16]]. That is guidance for an ice-contaminated tail, not a clean-airplane slip rule, and an iced airplane is no place for power-off 180 practice.

Why a slip is acceptable near the ground when a skid is not: a slipping airplane that stalls shows very little of the yaw that turns a skidding stall into a spin, and may simply tend to roll level [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

check.q: In a full-flap forward slip your learner sees the airspeed needle drop 12 knots and shoves the nose down. What is your likely diagnosis, and what do you teach?
check.a: The indicator may be reading wrong in the slip because of pitot and static location. Hold the slip attitude and judge by attitude, sound and feel [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]; reacting to erroneous airspeed is a listed slip error [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. Check the POH for limits on slips with flaps.

chunks.title: Crosswind: slip into the wind, sideslip to the touchdown

body.p: Crosswind (R2a): final is normally flown into the wind, so base usually has a crosswind and needs a drift correction [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. On final, a crab or a sideslip holds the path, and a forward slip may be used momentarily to steepen the descent [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]. In a crosswind, lower the upwind wing so the slip is into the wind; that makes it easier to stay on the original flight path [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Slipping in the same direction as the crosswind is a listed error [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

bullets: Correlate (S7): wind from the left, left wing down; wind from the right, right wing down [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

Transition (S7): when the round out begins, remove the forward slip [[24:186|AFH 9-15]], but in a crosswind keep the upwind wing down and use rudder to align the nose with the runway: the wing-low sideslip [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].
Keep the upwind wing down through the round out and increase the deflections as speed decays; touch down on the upwind main first [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
A late transition to the sideslip, and landing with the axis not parallel to the runway, are listed errors [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

body.p: Limits: if full opposite rudder cannot stop the turn at the bank needed, the wind is too strong for that runway [[24:188|AFH 9-17]]. Certification demonstrates control in a 90° crosswind up to 0.2 VSO [[24:190|AFH 9-19]].

callout.text: Why the ACS says no side drift: touching down while drifting side-loads the gear. As little as 10° of cornering angle makes a side load of half the weight on that tire, and a high-wing tricycle airplane can roll over past some angle [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

body.p: What to watch for: learners who level the wings to 'take out the slip' in a crosswind start drifting at once [[24:188|AFH 9-17]]. Teach that the same wing stays down from the slip to the touchdown, and only the nose moves.

check.q: Wind from the right. Your learner is forward-slipping on final with the left wing low. What is wrong, and what will you say?
check.a: That slip is with the wind, a listed error [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. Lower the right, upwind wing so the slip is into the wind and the path is easier to hold [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

chunks.title: Choosing the runway, the point and the path

callout.text: For any flight, the PIC must become familiar with runway lengths at airports of intended use and the takeoff and landing distance information [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]].

body.p: Pilot capability: the RMH sample personal minimums for a single-engine pilot include a 7-knot crosswind component and a 2,500-foot shortest runway [[30:16|RMH 2-4]]. It suggests adding at least 500 feet of runway at unfamiliar airports and subtracting at least 5 knots from wind limits under outside pressure, and warns not to adjust minimums to complete a specific flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

The point (S4): the runway numbers give no safety cushion for a mechanical problem or misjudgment; a point farther down the runway adds margin [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. The AIH says aiming and touchdown points should not be chosen mechanically: teach the learner to choose them from the airplane, the landing being made, the conditions and the expected performance [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. Application: on a short runway, check that the point plus 200 feet plus the landing roll still fits.

body.p: The path (S3): altitude, obstructions, wind, landing direction, surface and gradient, and landing distance all decide the pattern for a power-off approach [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. A pilot who overestimates gliding range may try to stretch over obstacles on final; it can be better to plan the approach over an unobstructed area [[24:354|AFH 18-5]].

callout.text: Teach pre-landing reconnaissance for unfamiliar landing areas, and in strong wind make sure your own skill is up to it [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

check.q: On a 2,600-foot grass strip your learner chooses the runway numbers as the point 'to leave lots of room.' What do you discuss?
check.a: The numbers give no cushion for a misjudgment or a mechanical problem; a point farther down adds margin [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. On a short soft strip, pick it from the expected performance [[25:193|AIH 10-9]] and check that point plus 200 feet plus the roll still fits [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]].

chunks.title: Windshear and wake turbulence with no power in hand

body.p: Windshear: a sudden, drastic change in wind speed or direction over a very small area, most dangerous near the ground. A headwind that becomes a tailwind cuts airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. On approach, a microburst can give a headwind, then a downdraft, then a tailwind that forces the airplane to the ground short of the runway; virga over an intense rain shaft or a ring of blowing dust may be the only clue [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

bullets: Near convective weather, treat a rapid airspeed gain as a possible sign of a coming loss and a reason to discontinue the approach [[28:273|AWH 22-18]].
Be ready to go around at the first indication; some microbursts cannot be escaped [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].
Application: a power-off glide has no power held in reserve. On a day with convective weather nearby, make it a normal power approach instead.

body.p: Wake turbulence: vortices are strongest behind an aircraft that is heavy, clean and slow [[34:147|AIM 7-4-3]]. They sink several hundred feet per minute and, within 100 to 200 feet of the ground, drift sideways at 2 or 3 knots [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]]. A light quartering tailwind needs maximum caution because it can move the vortices into the touchdown zone [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]]. Behind a larger aircraft landing on the same runway, stay at or above its final approach path, note its touchdown point and land beyond it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

callout.text: The AIM rule behind a larger aircraft on the same runway is to stay at or above its path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. A power-off 180 to a fixed point short of that touchdown point cannot meet it, so ask for a point beyond it, wait, or fly a normal approach. Application: the ACS treats a go-around for runway safety concerns beyond your control as not unsatisfactory (ACS Appendix 3).

check.q: A regional turboprop landed on your runway a minute ago with a light quartering tailwind. The examiner's point is short of where it touched down. What do you say?
check.a: Its vortices may sit in or drift into the touchdown zone [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]]. Ask for a point beyond its touchdown point and stay at or above its path [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]], or delay the maneuver.

body.p: Rejected landing and go-around: a normal maneuver for ATC, runway hazards, overtaking traffic, wind shear, wake turbulence, mechanical failure or an unstable approach. The instructor should stress early that any approach may end in a go-around [[24:181|AFH 9-10]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Delay comes from landing expectancy and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]], and in this maneuver both are strong, because the learner is trying to hit a point.

bullets: Power: full power, smoothly and without hesitation; carburetor heat off if applicable [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

Attitude: the airplane is trimmed for an idle glide. Full power makes the nose rise sharply and turn left, the setup for an elevator trim stall, which must be avoided in a real go-around [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Expect strong forward pressure and right rudder [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Configuration: flaps up in small steps after the descent stops; a sudden full retraction can let the airplane settle into the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Ground effect: its extra performance is borrowed and repaid on climbing out of it; climbing too early may leave the airplane unable to climb [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

head: Go-around trigger
Source
rows: Unstabilized below 300 feet AGL
Low and undershooting with any doubt about completing the approach
Sink rate becoming excessive (800 to 1,000 fpm is considered excessive)
Floating: cannot land in the first third of the runway, or drifting sideways
Nosewheel strikes first and the nose bounces up
Tempted to force the airplane onto the runway to avoid overshooting the point
[[24:198|AFH 9-27]] (ACS Appendix 3)

body.p: Land and hold short operations (LAHSO): you may accept only if you, as PIC, determine the airplane can safely land and stop within the Available Landing Distance (ALD) [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]]. The PIC has final authority to accept or decline and is expected to decline if it would compromise safety. The ALD is in the Chart Supplement, and preflight planning should decide which LAHSO combinations work for your airplane's required landing distance. Student pilots and pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not participate [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. Wind conditions are one of the AIM's examples of a reason to decline; tell ATC promptly, ideally before the clearance is issued. A LAHSO clearance does not rule out a rejected landing; keep separation and notify the controller [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

callout.text: Application of the AIM rule to land and stop within the ALD [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]]: in this Task the touchdown may legally be anywhere from the point to 200 feet beyond it (ACS AI.VII.O.S8), so the distance to plan is the point, plus 200 feet, plus the POH ground roll. If the hold-short point leaves no margin past that, decline before you start the maneuver.

check.q: Your learner goes around from a floating, long power-off approach and the nose shoots up as the throttle comes in. Why, and what should they have expected?
check.a: The airplane was trimmed nose-up for the idle glide, so full power makes the nose rise sharply toward an elevator trim stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Expect strong forward pressure and right rudder, then rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

chunks.title: Checklists, radio calls and collision hazards

bullets: Checklists (S1): complete the before-landing checklist on downwind, including gear extension in a retractable [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. Failure to lower the gear is a listed power-off error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

Engine: keep it warm and cleared during simulated emergency approaches [[24:200|AFH 9-29]], but using the throttle to extend the glide instead of merely clearing the engine is a listed error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].
After landing, positively identify the flap and gear controls before moving either; many accidents came from raising the gear instead of the flaps [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

Radio calls (S2): at a non-towered airport, announce downwind, base and final, for example 'On left base for runway [XX]' [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]], and communicate your position to other pattern traffic [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].

body.p: Collision hazards: most reported midair collisions happen on final or short final [[24:171|AFH 8-7]]. They happen mostly in daylight, between aircraft going the same direction, at or near uncontrolled airports below 1,000 feet [[24:170|AFH 8-6]]. Before turning final, make sure no aircraft is already established there; a rushed turn to gain spacing is good reason to go around [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. Aircraft on final have the right-of-way, and the lower of two landing aircraft has it but may not cut in front of or overtake one on final [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]. A pilot flying a VFR straight-in has no priority over pattern traffic [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.1]].

Application: once the throttle closes at the downwind key, your airplane descends early and turns base closer in than a normal pattern. Other pilots may not expect it, so the downwind and base calls matter more, and the learner must look for the straight-in and for traffic on a wider base before turning.

callout.text: Flight instructors were on board in 37 percent of the midair collisions in one study [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Make 'final clear, runway clear' a spoken item before every base-to-final turn.

check.q: Halfway down an idle base, your learner hears a Cessna report a 4-mile straight-in. Who has the right-of-way, and what do you coach?
check.a: An aircraft on final, or the lower of two landing aircraft, has it but may not cut in front of one on final [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]; the straight-in has no priority over pattern traffic [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.1]]. Find it, talk to it, and go around rather than rush the turn [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

chunks.title: Low altitude: stall, spin, CFIT, distraction and illusions

body.p: Low altitude maneuvering, stall and spin: gliding turns need more back pressure than a straight glide, but less rudder pressure than learners expect from powered flight [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. On a power-off approach, excess rudder banks the airplane, the pilot holds opposite aileron and adds back pressure, and a full cross-control condition develops. A stall there almost certainly means a rapid, unrecoverable spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Skidding turns to stretch the glide are a listed error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]. After a base-to-final overshoot, the safest action is a go-around; be reluctant to bank past 30° there and never skid [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

Sixty percent of stall/spin accidents happened during takeoff and landing, and most when the pilot's attention was diverted [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. CFIT often follows intentionally flying too low [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]; a low, stretched base over trees is exactly that. Visual illusions push the learner low: an upsloping runway, featureless terrain or water, and rain on the windscreen all can lead to a lower approach than desired [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

Distractions, task prioritization and loss of situational awareness: in overload a pilot works harder but gets less done and may fixate; stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Situational awareness includes the airplane's position and path, other aircraft and the environment [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. In this maneuver the point itself is the fixation: on short final, full attention goes to a good, safe landing, not to the point [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

head: Distraction trap
What it looks like
Defense
rows: Throttle confusion
Both hands near the throttle on a simulated engine failure
One person has complete control of the throttle, briefed before flight; many near accidents came from that doubt [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]
Instructor talking on final
Missed radio calls and traffic
Use only concise prompting on approach [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]
Teaching at the wrong time
Explaining technique when attention belongs on control
Do the teaching on the ground or before the approach, not in the turn to final; the AIH warns against teaching at an inappropriate time [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]
Disorientation from illusions
Learner settles low over featureless terrain or in rain
Expect it, check the altimeter, use visual glide path aids when available [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]]

check.q: Low on an idle base, your learner banks toward final but holds opposite aileron and a lot of inside rudder to 'keep the bank shallow.' What do you do and why?
check.a: Take it or call the go-around now. That is a cross-control condition in a gliding turn, and a stall there almost certainly becomes a rapid, unrecoverable spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: Ground brief: the POH glide speed (or 1.4 VSO), flap and slip limits, the point and why it was chosen, who has the throttle [[24:200|AFH 9-29]], and the go-around triggers. Build in blocks: a solid normal glide first, then abnormal glides [[24:84|AFH 3-23]], gliding turns with their reduced rudder pressures [[24:85|AFH 3-24]], then the 90° from base, then the 180° [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]. Do not introduce forced landings on a first lesson; emergency procedures go in after the learner knows normal operations [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

bullets: Demonstrate first, explaining the judgment calls aloud at the downwind key and on base, then let the learner fly. With a hard maneuver, be ready to take control, especially on the first attempts [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Do not teach it mechanically: coach power, control and configuration for what is happening on that approach, and teach how to choose the point [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].
Anticipate errors: the AIH says learners may understand not to trade a stable approach and safe landing for accuracy, but not yet be ready to apply it [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].
Vary the downwind altitude and the point between laps so the learner judges angles, not landmarks [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].
Let the learner fly the plan they chose so they see the result of their errors, and then explain and correct [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
End a simulated approach as soon as it is clear whether a safe landing is assured [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

head: Moment
Usually let the learner work it
Take it, or call the go-around
rows: Low on base
Shortens the base, delays flaps [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]
Raises the nose below glide speed or starts to skid [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
High on final
Adds flaps or slips into the wind [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Dives at the point with sink building toward 800 to 1,000 fpm [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Short final
Small corrections, eyes on the landing
Unstabilized below 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Flare
A short float
Forcing it on, or floating past the first third [[24:198|AFH 9-27]] [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]

callout.text: Eagerness to get down is one of the most common faults: learners arrive with too much speed, float and overshoot. Stress that a pilot cannot dive at a field and expect to land on it [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

body.p: When you take the controls, say it calmly and clearly, 'I have the flight controls.' Anxious learners can be very strong, and there is nothing to gain by fighting them [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: Your learner nails the 180° every time at your home field but is lost at a new airport. What went wrong in your teaching, according to the AFH?
check.a: The learner tied the key positions to landmarks at fixed heights. Both altitude and location should be varied as much as practical so the learner judges the glide, not a tree or crossroad [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

body.p: These come from the AFH lists for power-off accuracy approaches [[24:198|AFH 9-27]], descents and gliding turns [[24:85|AFH 3-24]] and the forward slip to a landing [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. On the checkride you analyze and correct common errors (ACS AI.VII.O.S9): name what you see, the likely cause, and the fix.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Downwind too far from the runway
Normal height at the key, but the point looks far away after the turn
Fly the normal pattern distance [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]; shorten the base and hold flaps [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]
Downwind overextended by a tailwind
Throttle closed late; long base, low all the way
Close the throttle abreast of the point [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]; turn base promptly
Inadequate drift correction on base
Base track curving toward or away from the runway
Crab to hold the track and read the wind from it [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]
Skidding turns to glide farther
Ball out, nose yawing into the turn, opposite aileron
Coordinated turns only; less rudder in gliding turns; go around if short [[24:85|AFH 3-24]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Gear not lowered (retractable)
Gear warning, no green lights
Before-landing checklist on downwind [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]
Stretching the glide
Nose up, airspeed below best glide, the spot rising in the windshield
Lower the nose to best glide; never stretch [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]
Premature flaps or gear
Steep and short early, low later
Hold full flaps until the point is assured [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]
Throttle used to stretch the glide
Power held beyond a brief clearing
Clear the engine only; if short, go around [[24:198|AFH 9-27]] [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]
Forcing it onto the runway
Pushing over to hit the point; flat or nosewheel-first touchdown
Accept a long landing or go around [[24:197|AFH 9-26]] [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]
Slip with the crosswind
Downwind wing low; drifting off the centerline
Lower the upwind wing [[24:184|AFH 9-13]] [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]
Late sideslip transition
Drift or crab at touchdown
Hold the upwind wing down through the round out [[24:188|AFH 9-17]]
Chasing the airspeed indicator
Pitch hunting, speed never settles
Set the glide attitude and trim; use sound and feel [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]

body.p: Causes behind the symptoms: the listed errors that leave a learner short are mostly made on downwind or in the turn to base (downwind too far out, a tailwind-overextended downwind, poor drift correction on base) [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]. Long approaches usually come from excess speed: diving at the field brings an appreciable increase in airspeed and a float [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]. So when you debrief, start where the energy went wrong, not where the airplane landed (application).

callout.text: It is always better to make a good landing away from the point than a poor landing on it [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

check.q: Your learner lands short on three laps in a row, and each time the spot was 'fine at the base key.' Where do you look first?
check.a: Before the base key: a downwind too far out, a tailwind-overextended downwind, or poor drift correction on base are all listed errors [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]. Watch the throttle point and the turn to base on the next lap.

scenario.title: Checkride prep on a gusty, busy afternoon
scenario.setup: Your commercial learner's checkride is in three days. You plan an hour of power-off 180s at a towered airport with crossing runways. Runway 27 is 4,000 feet and damp; wind 230 at 12 gusting 18. A business jet is on a 5-mile final for runway 33. Showers are building 15 miles southwest. The trainer's POH prohibits slips with flaps extended. Your learner says, 'I have to get these perfect today, I can't afford another lesson.'

questions.q: Before the first lap, what do you weigh about the wind, the runway and the learner?
questions.a: The crosswind against the demonstrated value (0.2 VSO) [[24:190|AFH 9-19]] and the learner's personal minimums, which outside pressure should tighten, not loosen [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. A damp runway raises hydroplaning risk if they land fast [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]].

questions.q: Which point do you ask the tower-cleared learner to use on runway 27, and why not the numbers?
questions.a: A point a little down the runway: the numbers leave no cushion for a misjudgment, and a point farther down adds margin [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. With the jet landing on 33, the plan must also keep you above its path where you cross it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

questions.q: On final with a left crosswind the learner is high. The POH prohibits slips with flaps and full flaps are out. What now?
questions.a: Follow the POH: slips with flaps may be limited for aerodynamic reasons [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Without a slip, the fix comes earlier: more path on base or earlier flaps [[24:196|AFH 9-25]], or a go-around if the sink would become excessive [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

questions.q: Tower offers 'cleared to land runway 27, hold short runway 33.' The intersection is 1,900 feet from the threshold. Your point is 900 feet and the POH ground roll is 650 feet. Accept?
questions.a: Application: 900 + 200 + 650 = 1,750 feet leaves only 150 feet on a damp, gusty runway with a learner flying, so decline. You may accept only if you determine the airplane can safely land and stop within the ALD [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]]; the PIC is expected to decline LAHSO that would compromise safety [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]], and wind is one of the AIM's reasons to decline; tell ATC promptly [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

questions.q: On the third lap the airspeed jumps 12 knots on base and the showers look closer. The learner is pleased to have 'extra energy.' What do you teach?
questions.a: Near convective weather a rapid airspeed gain may come before a loss and is a reason to discontinue the approach [[28:273|AWH 22-18]]. With idle power and no reserve, go around and end the power-off work for the day [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].

questions.q: Behind on time, the learner turns final low and starts a skidding turn while pleading to 'get just one good one.' How do you handle the moment and the rest of the lesson?
questions.a: Call the go-around now: a skidding turn while low invites a cross-control stall and spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Then end or change the lesson: the AIH says to terminate a lesson early if a learner is anxious about time pressure [[25:192|AIH 10-8]], and personal minimums are not adjusted to finish a flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

skills.do: Complete the before-landing checklist on downwind, including the gear in a retractable, and explain why it is done before the downwind key.
skills.practice: Fly the downwind flow and say each item aloud before reaching abeam the point [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

skills.do: Make the downwind, base and final calls (or follow ATC) while flying the early, close-in power-off pattern.
skills.practice: Script the calls for your home field and use them on every lap [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].

skills.do: Plan and follow a flightpath to the point considering altitude, wind, terrain and obstructions, explaining each judgment at the keys.
skills.practice: On each lap, say the plan for the base leg before closing the throttle [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

skills.do: Select the most suitable touchdown point for the wind, surface, obstructions and airplane limits, and explain why it is not just the numbers.
skills.practice: Pick a different point each lap and justify it in one sentence [[24:196|AFH 9-25]] [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

skills.do: Position the airplane on downwind parallel to the runway at normal pattern distance and close the throttle abreast of the point.
skills.practice: Use a wingtip or strut reference to mark 'abreast' and check the distance out each lap [[24:198|AFH 9-27]] [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].

skills.do: Configure correctly: glide speed or 1.4 VSO after the key, flaps in increments as the energy allows, 1.3 VSO on final, trimmed.
skills.practice: Practice the glide entry and flap steps with re-trim while talking [[24:197|AFH 9-26]] [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

skills.do: As necessary, slip into the crosswind on final and change to a sideslip before touchdown, explaining which wing stays down and why.
skills.practice: On crosswind days, practice slip-to-sideslip transitions at altitude, then in the pattern [[24:184|AFH 9-13]] [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

skills.do: Touch down at a proper pitch attitude, within 200 feet beyond or on the specified point with no side drift and with the airplane’s longitudinal axis aligned with and over the runway centerline or landing path, as applicable. (ACS AI.VII.O.S8) Do it while explaining, and go around rather than force it.
skills.practice: Have someone name the point on downwind; log each miss in feet short or long and what caused it [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors, usually a simulated error flown by the examiner as your learner: name it, its cause and the fix.
skills.practice: For each row of the error table, practice one sentence each for what you see, why, and what you say [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH, what is the real basis of all power-off accuracy approaches and landings?
options: Holding exactly 1.3 VSO from the downwind key to the flare
Flying a perfectly square pattern at the same altitude every lap
Judging height above the ground to within about fifty feet
Estimating the distance the airplane will glide
quiz.why: The ability to estimate gliding distance is the real basis of all power-off accuracy approaches [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

quiz.q: Your learner closes the throttle at the downwind key and the nose drops at once, so the glide starts steep and fast. What does the AFH say the entry should look like?
options: Add a notch of flaps first so the nose rises by itself while the speed bleeds off to glide speed
Lower the nose right away to hold the downwind airspeed, then let it slow down later on base
Hold altitude with back pressure until the speed decays to glide speed, then set the glide attitude and trim
Trim fully nose-up before closing the throttle so the airplane holds altitude with no back pressure
quiz.why: Close the throttle, hold altitude with back pressure until the speed decays to best glide, then set the attitude and trim [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Inadequate back pressure at entry, giving an overly steep glide, is a listed error [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

quiz.q: Once the throttle is closed at the downwind key, which control input can add total energy?
options: Lowering the nose to trade some height for airspeed toward best glide
None of them; with thrust below drag, total energy only drains
A short forward slip held into the wind on final approach
Retracting one notch of flaps to cut the drag on the airplane
quiz.why: The throttle controls total energy; with thrust less than drag it decreases. The elevator only trades altitude and speed, and drag devices can only add drag [[24:90|AFH 4-4]]. Retracting flaps does not add energy and can cause a sudden loss of lift [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

quiz.q: Your learner wants to fly minimum sink speed on base 'to stay up longer' and reach the point. What does the AFH say about that speed?
options: It is a few knots faster than best glide and gives a flatter glide path
It covers the most distance because the airplane loses height at the lowest rate
It is the same as best glide speed in most light single-engine airplanes
It keeps the airplane aloft longest but covers less distance than best glide
quiz.why: Minimum sink maximizes time aloft, is generally a few knots below best glide, and results in less distance traveled [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Best glide gives the greatest distance [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].

quiz.q: A larger aircraft has just landed. When its vortices sink to within 100 to 200 feet of the ground, what does the AIM say they tend to do?
options: Rise back up to the larger aircraft's flight path within a minute or two
Move sideways over the ground at about 2 or 3 knots
Break up at once when they reach ground effect near the runway
Stay over the larger aircraft's touchdown point until they decay
quiz.why: Near the ground (within 100 to 200 feet) the vortices tend to move laterally at 2 or 3 knots [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]]; a light quartering tailwind can carry them into the touchdown zone [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

quiz.q: Your learner puts out the first 10° of flaps on base and the airplane balloons a little. What does the AFH say causes that?
options: Up to about 15°, flaps add mostly lift with little drag, so the airplane tends to balloon
The first notch of flaps always moves the center of gravity aft enough to raise the nose by itself
Small flap angles add so much drag that the learner pulls back to hold the speed
Partial flaps blank the elevator, so the airplane pitches up until full flaps are set
quiz.why: Flap deflection up to 15° mainly produces lift with minimal drag, and the airplane tends to balloon; beyond 15° drag rises sharply [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

quiz.q: During a simulated power-off approach, when does the AFH say the instructor should end it?
options: As soon as it can be determined whether or not a safe landing is assured
Only after the airplane has touched down on or past the point the learner chose
At exactly 500 feet AGL on every lap, whatever the approach looks like
When the learner has finished the full emergency checklist out loud
quiz.why: Every simulated emergency landing approach is terminated as soon as it can be determined whether a safe landing is assured, and never continued to an undue hazard [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

quiz.q: Your learner goes around from a long float with full flaps out. How should the flaps come up?
options: All at once as the power comes in, to get rid of the drag quickly
Not until reaching pattern altitude, so the climb stays steep
In small steps after the descent stops, as the AFM/POH recommends
First the gear, then all of the flaps, in every airplane
quiz.why: After the descent is stopped, retract flaps partially or to the takeoff setting as recommended, in small increments; a sudden full retraction can let the airplane settle into the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

quiz.q: After an idle glide trimmed nose-up, what is the main pitch hazard when your learner goes around?
options: The nose rises sharply and turns left toward an elevator trim stall
The nose drops sharply as soon as power comes in
The airplane yaws right and needs left rudder pressure
The flaps creep up on their own as full power builds airflow over them
quiz.why: Full power with nose-up landing trim makes the nose rise sharply and turn left, the elevator trim stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

quiz.q: The AIH uses the power-off 180° as an example in its landing-risk section. What does it warn instructors to expect?
options: Learners may know not to trade safety for accuracy but not yet apply it
Learners cannot fly it safely until after their commercial knowledge test
Learners should practice it solo first so they are not distracted by you
Learners always land long because they fear landing short of the point
quiz.why: Instructors should anticipate landing errors; learners may understand not to sacrifice a stable approach and safe landing for accuracy but might not be ready to apply that knowledge [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

final_quiz.q: At the base key your learner is 10 knots above glide speed and clearly lower than usual. Using the AFH energy matrix, what is this, and what fix works with the throttle closed?
options: Too little total energy; lower the nose to gain speed, then add flaps
A distribution error; raise the nose toward best glide to trade speed for path
Too much total energy; slip immediately to lose the extra speed
A distribution error; lower the nose further so the glide gets flatter
final_quiz.why: Lower-and-faster is an energy distribution error, fixed with the elevator [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]. Above best glide, pitching up reduces airspeed and shallows the descent angle [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

final_quiz.q: At an unfamiliar airport with an upsloping runway, every power-off approach your learner flies ends short and low. What does the PHAK point to?
options: The upslope adds a tailwind component on final, so the glide covers less ground than planned
The upslope creates an illusion of being lower than you are, so pilots fly a higher approach
The upslope creates an illusion of being higher than you are, so pilots fly a lower approach
The upslope makes the airplane float, so learners pull the throttle back too soon
final_quiz.why: An upsloping runway or terrain can create the illusion of greater height, and a pilot who does not recognize it flies a lower approach [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]. Anticipate it and use visual glide path aids when available [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner taps the throttle up to 1,500 rpm at the base key and holds it for 15 seconds 'to clear the engine.' What do you tell them?
options: That is the listed error of using throttle to stretch the glide
That is fine, as long as the power comes off before turning final
That is too little; clear with full power for at least 20 seconds
That is fine, since clearing the engine is required on every power-off lap
final_quiz.why: Keep the engine warm and cleared [[24:200|AFH 9-29]], but using the throttle to increase the glide instead of merely clearing the engine is a listed error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

final_quiz.q: You are instructing in a single-engine turboprop whose checklist calls for feathering after an engine failure. How do you fly the power-off 180 in training?
options: Feather the propeller on downwind, exactly as the emergency checklist tells you to
Do not feather; set enough power to give the performance expected when feathered
Use flight idle all the way, whatever the descent rate turns out to be
Skip the Task, because the ACS excludes turboprop airplanes from it
final_quiz.why: In training, the propeller is not feathered; set sufficient power to provide the performance expected with it feathered [[24:196|AFH 9-25]] (ACS Appendix 3).

final_quiz.q: The examiner asks: 'R7 says tail stalls with flaps. What do the FAA handbooks tell you about that risk in a clean airplane during a forward slip?' Which answer is accurate?
options: The AFH limits all slips with flaps to 30 seconds to keep the tail from stalling
The PHAK says any slip with more than 15° of flaps will stall the tail in a trainer
The AFH says to retract the flaps to the previous setting whenever you slip with them
Only that slips with flaps may be limited for aerodynamic reasons; follow the POH
final_quiz.why: The AFH says there may be recommendations or limitations on slips with flaps for aerodynamic reasons and to consult the AFM/POH [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]; flaps change downwash on the tail [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. The flap-retraction recovery is IFH icing guidance [[23:93|IFH 4-16]].

final_quiz.q: Wind from the left. Your learner forward-slips with the left wing low and, at the round out, levels the wings to 'take the slip out.' What happens next?
options: Nothing; leveling the wings is correct at the round out
The airplane turns left toward the wind and lands in a crab
The airplane drifts right and touches down sideways
The airplane balloons because the slip drag is suddenly gone
final_quiz.why: If the wings are leveled the airplane starts drifting and touches down drifting; keep the upwind wing down through the round out [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

final_quiz.q: Tower clears you to land and hold short of a crossing runway 1,600 feet from your threshold. Your point is 1,000 feet in and the POH roll is 600 feet. What do you do?
options: Accept, since the roll ends exactly at the hold-short line
Accept, then plan to land exactly on the point to save the room you need
Decline only if the controller has not given you the ALD
Decline, since point plus 200 feet plus the roll is 1,800 feet
final_quiz.why: 1,000 + 200 + 600 = 1,800 feet, which exceeds 1,600 feet. Accept only if the airplane can safely land and stop within the ALD [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]], and decline LAHSO that would compromise safety [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]; the ACS window allows touchdown up to 200 feet past the point (ACS AI.VII.O.S8).

final_quiz.q: Near building showers, the airspeed jumps 15 knots on your learner's idle base. They say, 'Free energy, I'll make the point easily.' What is right?
options: Use the extra speed to stretch the glide all the way to the point
Treat it as a warning of a coming loss and discontinue
Slip immediately to get rid of the extra airspeed
Lower full flaps now to hold the planned glide angle
final_quiz.why: A rapid or large airspeed increase near convective weather may precede a decrease and is a reason to discontinue the approach [[28:273|AWH 22-18]].

final_quiz.q: On your CFI checkride you misjudge the turn to base and see you will touch down about 350 feet past the point. What is right, and how is it graded?
options: Land long anyway; the examiner grades only the approach itself
Force it on near the point; the ACS allows that in any crosswind
Go around: unsatisfactory, but forcing it on is never acceptable
Go around; any go-around in this Task is graded as satisfactory
final_quiz.why: Forcing the airplane onto the runway to avoid overshooting is a listed error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]. A go-around for inability to meet the tolerances is unsatisfactory, but no one may force a landing to complete the Task (ACS Appendix 3).

final_quiz.q: Teaching power-off 180s, you notice you talk through every correction on final, and on the last lap you both missed a tower call. What does the AIH say?
options: Use only concise prompting on approach; excess coaching can cause missed calls
Keep talking, since constant coaching on final is how the learner builds judgment
Stop all talking from the downwind key on, and save every comment for the debrief
Take the radios yourself so the learner can listen to the coaching in peace
final_quiz.why: Excessive teaching and coaching on final can cause missed radio transmissions; use only concise prompting on approach to landings [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

final_quiz.q: On a wet runway your learner plans to touch down 15 knots fast 'for safety' at the end of a power-off 180. What is the problem?
options: None; extra speed protects against a stall in the flare
Extra speed raises hydroplaning risk and floats past the point
Extra speed only matters on runways shorter than 2,500 feet
Wet runways need a forward slip held all the way to the touchdown
final_quiz.why: Landing at a higher speed raises the hydroplaning risk [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]], and excess approach speed causes floating well past the point [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].

final_quiz.q: During your demonstration the learner rests a hand on the throttle 'just in case.' At 300 feet you decide to go around. What should have been settled on the ground?
options: That whoever reaches it first will make the go-around
That the learner takes over the throttle below 500 feet
That the throttle is locked with the friction knob
That one person has complete control of the throttle at all times
final_quiz.why: Either the instructor or the pilot should have complete control of the throttle, with no doubt about who; many near accidents came from that misunderstanding [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner keeps arriving at the edge of the runway fast, floating far past the point. Which AFH fault is this, and how do you address it?
options: Stretching the glide; teach a slower glide speed on the base leg
Downwind too close; move the downwind leg farther out
Premature flaps; hold every notch of flaps until short final
Eagerness to get down; you can't dive at a field and land on it
final_quiz.why: Eagerness to get down is one of the most common faults: too much speed means floating and overshooting, and instructors should stress that pilots cannot dive at a field and expect to land on it [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

takeaways: You touch down on the point or within 200 feet beyond it, with no drift and the axis on the centerline, while explaining (ACS AI.VII.O.S8).
Gliding distance judgment is the whole maneuver, and the same skill picks a field after an engine failure [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
With the throttle closed, no control can add total energy: plan slightly high and spend the extra with drag and path [[24:90|AFH 4-4]] [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].
Below best glide, the nose goes down to go farther; never stretch the glide or retract the flaps [[24:195|AFH 9-24]] [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].
Slip into the wind, keep that wing down into the sideslip, and respect POH slip limits [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
A go-around for missing the tolerance is unsatisfactory, but forcing a landing is never acceptable (ACS Appendix 3).
Vary the keys, coach briefly on final, and expect learners to know the rule before they can apply it [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].
cfi_notes: The FI ACS Appendix 3 note for this Task is printed under the headings 'VIII. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds' and 'Task M. Power-Off 180° Accuracy Approach and Landing (ASEL, ASES)' (FI ACS p. 102), but in the Task list it is Area VII, Task O (AI.VII.O). The text (turboprop power setting, go-around grading, never force a landing) is the one to brief.

The AFH stabilized-approach list includes a power setting not below the AFM minimum for approach [[24:177|AFH 9-6]], while the power-off approach fixes power at idle [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. The AFH does not reconcile the two. Teach the other elements and the 300-foot rule, and check the POH for any idle-power note.

R7 'tail stalls with flaps': for a clean airplane the sources only say there may be limits on slips with flaps 'for aerodynamic reasons' [[24:184|AFH 9-13]] and that flaps change the downwash and tail-down force [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. Tailplane stall symptoms and the 'retract flaps to the previous setting' recovery appear only in icing material [[23:93|IFH 4-16]]; that does not conflict with the AFH rule never to retract flaps to reach the spot [[24:197|AFH 9-26]], because it covers an iced tail. Tell the examiner that honestly and teach the POH limit (see the AI.VII.M lesson).
The 1.4 VSO glide speed is the AFH fallback only when the manufacturer gives no glide speed [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]; most POHs publish one. Use the POH number.
Hydroplaning formulas differ: the PHAK uses 9 times the square root of tire pressure [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]], the AFH 8.6 [[24:208|AFH 9-37]]. Either way, landing fast raises the risk.

The AFH advice to let the learner fly the field first chosen, so the instructor can explain the results of errors, is written for simulated emergency landings [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. It applies well to the 180° as long as you stay inside the go-around triggers.

AIH 10-9 names this maneuver directly as one where the instructor should anticipate errors [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. Examiners know that page; be ready to say what errors you expect and when you would step in.
The AFH says 'student' and the AIH says 'learner.' Same person.
gaps: Best glide speed, flap limits, and any limits on slips (time, fuel quantity, flaps) are airplane-specific: use the POH/AFM.
No source gives tower phraseology for requesting or flying a power-off 180° at a towered airport; agree it with the controller.

Tail stalls with flaps during a slip: for a clean airplane the sources say only that flaps change tail downwash and tail-down force and that slips with flaps may be limited for aerodynamic reasons; tailplane stall symptoms and recovery are given only for ice on the tail.
No source gives a way to calculate gliding distance in wind beyond 'a tailwind glides farther, a headwind less far' [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
No source describes how the key positions and the angle to the point look from the right seat; build your own references in practice.

activities.title: True or false: judging the power-off 180
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: On a power-off approach, pitch is used to control airspeed, and that also changes the glide angle.
cards.why: True. Power is fixed at idle, pitch adjusts airspeed, and that also changes the descent angle [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

cards.s: Square patterns are required on a power-off approach, because they show good planning.
cards.why: False. Square patterns demonstrate good planning but are not required and may not suit every approach [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

cards.s: The key position is the main objective of the maneuver.
cards.why: False. It is merely a convenient point in the air from which to judge what to do [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

cards.s: Closing the throttle with the same airspeed and height each time makes the maneuver more predictable.
cards.why: True. Starting with the same energy each time makes it more predictable [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

cards.s: Initial flaps may be extended before the base key position if needed.
Gliding turns need more rudder pressure than powered turns, because the slipstream is gone.
cards.why: False. Rudder pressures are reduced in gliding turns, and learners used to powered flight tend to use too much [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

activities.title: Power-off numbers
activities.intro: Work each one out, then type your answer.

items.q: In simulated power-failure training the AFH has you start the power-up recovery at a 10 percent lead. Your learner's glide is descending at 700 fpm. How many feet above the target altitude should power start coming in?
items.why: 10 percent of the descent rate: 0.10 x 700 = 70 feet (the AFH example is 100 feet at 1,000 fpm) [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

items.q: VSO is 48 knots and your final approach target is 1.3 VSO. Using the AFH stabilized-approach band of +10/-5 knots, what is the lowest speed that still counts as stabilized?
The POH landing distance is 1,200 feet at the weight in the chart. Today you are 10 percent heavier. About what landing distance should you plan?
items.why: Landing distance varies in direct proportion to gross weight: 10 percent more weight gives 10 percent more distance, 1,200 x 1.10 = 1,320 feet [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

items.q: VSO is 48 knots. What crosswind velocity did certification demonstrate for a 90° crosswind?
Your POH landing distance is 1,350 feet, and you must land with a 10-knot tailwind. About what landing distance now?
items.why: A 10-knot tailwind adds about 21 percent: 1,350 x 1.21 = 1,633.5 feet [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

activities.title: Coaching a 180° that goes sideways
activities.intro: You are instructing a commercial learner in a fixed-gear trainer. Point: the 1,000-foot markers on runway 36. Wind 330 at 10. Right seat, you have briefed that the learner has the throttle. The lesson unfolds one decision at a time.

steps.s: On downwind the learner says, 'I'll close it a little past the markers so I don't come up short.' What do you say?
options: 'Good idea, a little extra helps you avoid coming up short'
'Close it abreast of the point and judge from there'
'Close it now, well before the markers, to be safe on the glide'
'Leave some power in until base so you cannot come up short'
steps.why: The throttle closes abreast of the point at the downwind key [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]. Flying past it lengthens the glide, and some power left in turns it into a different maneuver.

steps.s: On base the learner holds an unusually large crab to the left and says nothing. What do you ask?
options: 'Why are you crabbing at all instead of flying the track?'
'What does that crab tell you about the wind on final?'
'Can you level the wings and use rudder to hold the track?'
'Shall we add full flaps now to make the crab easier to hold?'
steps.why: The crab needed on base shows wind strength and direction and helps plan the turn to final and the flaps [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]. A question gets the learner thinking aloud [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

steps.s: Rolling out on final the learner is high with partial flaps. The wind is from the left. Which coaching fits?
options: 'Dive at the point and level off just before the flare'
'Raise the flaps and hold the speed for a flatter path'
'Add flaps as needed, or a brief slip, left wing down'
'Slip right wing down, away from the wind, to lose height'
steps.why: When high, lower flaps as required or slip [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]; slip into the wind by lowering the upwind (left) wing [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

steps.s: Short final, on speed and on path, the learner says, 'Watch me nail the point,' and stares at it. What do you say?
options: 'Good, keep your eyes on the point all the way down'
'Eyes on the landing now, not on the selected point'
'Add a bit of power to make sure you reach the point'
'Slip now so you land right on the point you picked'
steps.why: On short final, full attention goes to a good, safe landing rather than the selected spot; late adjustments are not appropriate [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]. Use a short prompt only [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

steps.s: The float carries the airplane toward the point plus 200 feet, and the learner starts pushing forward to 'get it on.' What now?
options: 'Push harder, we are almost on the runway anyway'
'Let it float, we are fine on the runway length'
'Go around: full power, forward pressure, right rudder'
'Hold it level and wait for it to settle on its own'
steps.why: Forcing it onto the runway is a listed error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]. Go around; expect the nose-up trim to pitch the nose up with full power [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
